metadata.scope: e_macedonia (all baronies across k_hellas and k_thessalonika)
metadata.hierarchy_note: hierarchy reflects data/ck3_title_tree.json (save-derived de jure tree including x_script_* dynamic titles); downstream localisation/historicity mods should key on barony_key and join against their target landed_titles tree.

schema_notes.modern_name: Clean modern/vanilla English display name of the audited settlement or holding.
schema_notes.hierarchy: De jure title hierarchy from data/ck3_title_tree.json (empire, kingdom, duchy, county, holding_type).
schema_notes.first_mention_year: Integer year of earliest documented attestation (negative values = BCE; null if no pre-modern attestation was identified).
schema_notes.first_mention_attestation: Summary of the earliest documented textual or epigraphic attestation (or unattested status).
schema_notes.is_historical_867: Boolean: true iff first_mention_year is known and <= 867 CE for the audited barony name.
schema_notes.named_after_post_867_person: Boolean: true if the title name incorporates a person, saint, or dynasty post-dating 867 CE.
schema_notes.eponym_details: Explanatory text for any eponymous origin (both pre-867 and post-867 eponyms); null if not eponymous or unrecorded.
schema_notes.natural_proper_name: Object indicating whether the title derives from a hydronym, oronym, choronym, or topographic_feature.
schema_notes.morphemes: List of constituent roots/morphemes with form, language, language_code (ISO 639-3 / ISO 639-5), and English translation.
schema_notes.etymology_analysis: Linguistic and historical etymology of the audited barony name.
schema_notes.older_name_by_867: Object indicating whether a distinct older name strictly attested <= 867 CE exists for the same site or immediate predecessor.
schema_notes.source_url: Primary reference URL (typically Wikipedia or regional historical encyclopedia), or null if unavailable.

b_patras.first_mention_attestation: Herodotus, Histories 1.145 (c. 440 BCE), listing Patrees (Patrai) among the twelve Achaean cities.
b_patras.eponym_details: Named after the mythological Achaean founder Patreus (Pausanias, Description of Greece 7.18.5).
b_patras.etymology_analysis: Derived from Ancient Greek Patrai (Πάτραι, plural), traditionally traced by Pausanias to the eponymous Achaean hero Patreus; Latinized as Patrae and adapted in Medieval/Modern Greek as Patra/Patras.

b_vostitsa.first_mention_attestation: Chronicle of the Morea / establishment of the Frankish Barony of Vostitsa (c. 1209 CE).
b_vostitsa.etymology_analysis: Medieval Greek Vostitza (Βοστίτζα) is a Slavic-derived toponym that replaced ancient Aigion in the Middle Ages (commonly linked to South Slavic *vostan 'garden' or *vostitsa), first securely attested in the 13th-century Frankish Barony of Vostitsa.

older_name_by_867.notes: Ancient Aigion (Latin Aegium) occupied the exact site and was restored as the modern name Aigio in the 19th century.

b_andravida.first_mention_attestation: Chronicle of the Morea (1205–1208 CE), recording Andravida as the capital of the Frankish Principality of Achaea; Latin bishopric attested 1212 CE.
b_andravida.etymology_analysis: Medieval toponym (Greek Ανδραβίδα, French Andreville) of uncertain pre-1204 origin, first emerging in historical records after the Fourth Crusade (1205 CE) as the unfortified capital of the Principality of Achaea.

older_name_by_867.notes: No distinct pre-867 CE settlement name is attested for the specific site of Andravida (ancient Elis lay ~15 km southeast).

b_kalavryta.first_mention_attestation: Chronicle of the Morea / establishment of the Frankish Barony of Kalavryta (c. 1208–1209 CE).
b_kalavryta.etymology_analysis: From Medieval Greek Kalavryta (Καλάβρυτα), literally 'good springs' (kalos 'good' + vrysis 'spring/water'), first documented as a baronial seat after the Frankish conquest in 1208–1209 CE.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Polybius, Histories 4.17–21 (2nd century BCE, recording events of 220 BCE)
older_name_by_867.notes: Modern Kalavryta was built near/on the site of ancient Arcadian/Achaean Cynaetha (Kynaitha).

b_corinth.first_mention_attestation: Homer, Iliad 2.570 (c. 8th century BCE) as Korinthos; also attested in Mycenaean Linear B (ko-ri-to, c. 1200 BCE).
b_corinth.eponym_details: Mythologically linked to Corinthus, son of Zeus or Marathon (Pausanias 2.1.1), though linguistically pre-Greek.
b_corinth.etymology_analysis: Pre-Greek substrate toponym Korinthos (Κόρινθος) featuring the characteristic -nth- suffix, continuously attested from Mycenaean Linear B and Homeric epic through the Byzantine era.

b_nikli.first_mention_attestation: Chronicle of the Morea / establishment of the Frankish Barony of Nikli (c. 1209 CE); predecessor form Amyklion appears from the 10th–11th century.
b_nikli.etymology_analysis: Medieval Greek Nikli (Νίκλι) developed by aphaeresis and metathesis/assimilation from Amyklion/Amykli (Ἀμύκλιον), a middle Byzantine name (attested 10th–11th c.) applied to the site of ancient Tegea.

older_name_by_867.notes: Nikli stood directly on the site of ancient Tegea, attested from Homer through the Council of Chalcedon (451 CE).

b_argos.eponym_details: Mythologically associated with Argos, son of Zeus and Niobe, though etymologically a topographic/pre-Greek term.
b_argos.etymology_analysis: Ancient Greek Argos (Ἄργος), explained by Strabo (8.6.9) as a Pelasgian/archaic word for 'plain' (describing the Argive plain), continuously attested from the Bronze Age and Homer onward.

b_damala.first_mention_attestation: Post-1204 Frankish conquest / Chronicle of the Morea (c. 1212 CE, when the Argolid and Damala passed to the de la Roche family).

morphemes.translation: uncertain (possibly from damalis 'heifer' or personal/family name Damalas)

b_damala.etymology_analysis: Medieval Greek Damala (Δαμαλᾶ, French Damalet), which replaced ancient Troezen in the Middle Ages and became part of the Frankish Barony of Veligosti–Damala in the 13th century.

older_name_by_867.notes: Damala is the medieval name for the site of ancient Troezen (Troizen).

b_mistra.first_mention_attestation: Chronicle of the Morea (1249 CE), recording the construction of the fortress of Myzithras/Mistra by William II of Villehardouin.

morphemes.translation: uncertain (possibly from myzithra 'whey cheese' hill shape or a personal name Myzithras)

b_mistra.etymology_analysis: Founded in 1249 CE on Mount Myzithras (Μυζηθρᾶς, shortened to Μυστρᾶς / Mistra) by William II of Villehardouin; etymology is debated between a local landowner's name and the conical hill's resemblance to myzithra cheese.

older_name_by_867.notes: Mistra was founded as a new fortress in 1249 CE; nearby Sparta/Lacedaemonia is already a separate barony (b_lacedaemonia) in e_macedonia.

b_monemvasia.first_mention_attestation: Willibald's Hodoeporicon (c. 723–728 CE), the oldest surviving mention of Monemvasia, founded in the late 6th century CE.
b_monemvasia.etymology_analysis: From Byzantine Greek Monemvasia (Μονεμβασία), compounded from mone ('single') + emvasis ('entrance'), referring to the narrow causeway linking the rock island fortress to the Laconian mainland.

b_lacedaemonia.first_mention_attestation: Homer, Iliad 2.581 (c. 8th century BCE) as Lakedaimon; also attested in Mycenaean Linear B (ra-ke-da-mi-ni-jo).
b_lacedaemonia.eponym_details: Mythologically named after Lacedaemon, son of Zeus and Taygete.
b_lacedaemonia.etymology_analysis: Classical Greek Lakedaimon (Λακεδαίμων, Latinized Lacedaemonia), the official ancient and medieval Byzantine name (Lakedaimonia) for Sparta and its Laconian territory.

b_karytaina.first_mention_attestation: Treaty of Sapienza (1209 CE) and Chronicle of the Morea, establishing the Frankish Barony of Karytaina.
b_karytaina.etymology_analysis: Medieval toponym Karytaina (Καρύταινα) of uncertain origin (variously linked to Slavic or Greek roots), unknown in sources before the 1205–1209 CE Frankish conquest.

older_name_by_867.notes: Karytaina occupies a hill near/at the site of ancient Arcadian Brenthe, already in ruins when described by Pausanias.

b_arcadia.first_mention_attestation: Middle Byzantine sources from the 10th–11th century CE onward, when Kyparissia became known as Arkadia.
b_arcadia.etymology_analysis: The regional choronym Arkadia (Ἀρκαδία) was transferred to coastal Kyparissia in the Middle Byzantine period (attested 10th–11th c. CE) due to refugees migrating from inland Arcadia during Slavic raids.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Homer, Iliad 2.593 (c. 8th century BCE, as Kyparissēeis); Strabo & Pausanias (Kyparissia)
older_name_by_867.notes: Ancient Kyparissia was renamed Arkadia in the 10th–11th century and resumed its ancient name after 1825.

b_kalamata.first_mention_attestation: 10th-century Byzantine document and the 11th-century Life of Saint Nikon the Metanoeite.

morphemes.translation: toponymic suffix (or from kalomata 'fair-eyed' Virgin Mary)

b_kalamata.etymology_analysis: First attested in the 10th century CE as Kalamata (Καλαμάτα), either derived from ancient Messenian Calamae ('reeds') or from a medieval church of the Panagia Kalomata ('fair-eyed').

older_name_by_867.notes: Medieval Kalamata Castle stands directly on the acropolis of ancient Pharae (Pharai).

b_modon.first_mention_attestation: First attested as the Venetian/Frankish form 'Modon' in 1125 CE (following Venetian Doge Domenico Michiel's 1124–1125 expedition and 12th-century Italian/Crusader sources).
b_modon.eponym_details: Mythologically linked by Pausanias to Mothone, daughter of Oeneus, or the harbour rock Mothon.
b_modon.etymology_analysis: Venetian/Frankish Modon is the direct medieval Romance phonological adaptation of Byzantine/Ancient Greek Mothone / Methone (Μοθώνη / Μεθώνη), continuously attested from Classical antiquity.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Thucydides, History of the Peloponnesian War 2.25.1 (431 BCE, as Methone); Pausanias 4.35 (as Mothone)
older_name_by_867.notes: The ancient Greek and Middle Byzantine city was called Methone / Mothone (Μεθώνη / Μοθώνη) prior to the Venetian/Frankish adaptation 'Modon' attested from 1125 CE.

b_abydos.first_mention_attestation: Homer, Iliad 2.836 (c. 8th century BCE); Milesian colony founded c. 670 BCE.
b_abydos.etymology_analysis: Ancient Hellespontine city Abydos (Ἄβυδος), of pre-Greek (likely Thracian or Anatolian) origin, attested in Homer and continuously occupied as a Byzantine customs station.

b_lampsakos.first_mention_attestation: Herodotus, Histories 5.117 and 6.37 (c. 440 BCE); colonized by Phocaea/Miletus in the 7th century BCE.
b_lampsakos.eponym_details: Mythologically named after Lampsake, a local Bebrycian princess who aided Phocaean colonists.
b_lampsakos.etymology_analysis: Ancient Greek Lampsakos (Λάμψακος), a major Hellespontine polis colonized in the 7th century BCE (earlier called Pityusa), continuously attested through Roman and Byzantine times.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Strabo, Geographica 13.1.18 (c. 20 CE) and Pliny the Elder, Naturalis Historia 5.141
older_name_by_867.notes: Ancient Greek sources record that Lampsakos was earlier called Pityusa/Pityoussa ('pine-clad') prior to Phocaean colonization.

b_ilion.first_mention_attestation: Homer, Iliad 1.71 (c. 8th century BCE) as Ilion / Ilios; corresponds to Hittite Wilusa (13th century BCE).
b_ilion.eponym_details: Mythologically named after Ilus, legendary founder of Troy.
b_ilion.etymology_analysis: Ancient Greek Ilion (Ἴλιον, earlier *Wilion with digamma), derived from Bronze Age Anatolian Wilusa and continuously attested from Homer through the Byzantine bishopric of Ilion.

b_alexandriatroas.first_mention_attestation: Strabo, Geography 13.1.26 (recording Lysimachus's renaming of Antigonia to Alexandria Troas in 301 BCE).
b_alexandriatroas.eponym_details: Renamed in 301 BCE by Lysimachus in memory of Alexander III (the Great) of Macedon.
b_alexandriatroas.etymology_analysis: Hellenistic Greek Alexandreia Troas (Ἀλεξάνδρεια Τρωάς, 'Alexandria of the Troad'), renamed in 301 BCE from Antigonia Troas (founded 306 BCE) and attested through Late Antiquity and Byzantine bishopric lists.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Strabo, Geographica 13.1.26 (recording its foundation as Antigonia by Antigonus I Monophthalmus in 306 BCE)
older_name_by_867.notes: Founded as Antigonia Troas by Antigonus I Monophthalmus in 306 BCE before Lysimachus renamed it Alexandria Troas in 301 BCE.

b_pagaea.first_mention_attestation: Anna Komnene, Alexiad (c. 1148 CE), referring to the Byzantine coastal fortress as Pigas / Pegai.
b_pagaea.etymology_analysis: Latinized/game adaptation of Medieval Greek Pegai (Πηγαί, Latin Pegae, 'Springs'), the Middle Byzantine fortress name (attested 12th c. CE) for ancient Priapos on the Propontis.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Arrian, Anabasis 1.12.7 (recording Alexander's capture in 334 BCE); Strabo, Geography 13.1.12
older_name_by_867.notes: Ancient Mysian polis Priapos (modern Karabiga) occupied the exact site before being renamed Pegai in the Middle Byzantine period.

b_chios.first_mention_attestation: Homer, Odyssey 3.170 (c. 8th century BCE); also attested in Mycenaean Linear B (ki-si-wi-jo).
b_chios.eponym_details: Mythologically linked to Chios, son of Poseidon (Pausanias 7.4.8).

morphemes.translation: island name (possibly from Phoenician 'mastic' or pre-Greek)

b_chios.etymology_analysis: Ancient Greek Chios (Χίος), naming both the northern Aegean island and its chief polis, attested since Mycenaean Linear B and Homer.

b_samos.first_mention_attestation: Homer, Odyssey 4.671 and Homeric Hymn to Apollo 41 (c. 8th–7th century BCE).

morphemes.translation: height, high place by the shore (Strabo 10.2.17)

b_samos.etymology_analysis: Ancient Greek Samos (Σάμος), explained by Strabo as an archaic/pre-Greek term meaning 'heights' (shared with Samothrace and Cephallenia/Same), naming the eastern Aegean island and its polis.

b_mytilene.first_mention_attestation: Fragments of Alcaeus and Sappho (c. 600 BCE) and Herodotus, Histories 1.160 (c. 440 BCE); founded in the 11th century BCE.
b_mytilene.eponym_details: Mythologically named after Mytilene, daughter of Macareus (Diodorus Siculus 5.81).
b_mytilene.etymology_analysis: Ancient Aeolic Greek Mytilene (Μυτιλήνη, possibly of Anatolian/pre-Greek origin), the principal city of Lesbos, attested from the Archaic lyric poets and Herodotus onward.

b_lemnos.first_mention_attestation: Homer, Iliad 1.593 (c. 8th century BCE); also attested in Mycenaean Linear B (ra-mi-ni-ja).
b_lemnos.etymology_analysis: Pre-Greek (possibly Tyrsenian/Lemnian) island name Lemnos (Λῆμνος), attested from Mycenaean Linear B and Homeric epic through the Byzantine period.

b_skyros.etymology_analysis: Ancient Greek Skyros (Σκῦρος), traditionally linked to Greek skyros ('stone/chippings', reflecting the island's rugged limestone terrain), attested since the Iliad.

b_naxos.first_mention_attestation: Herodotus, Histories 5.28 and 6.96 (c. 440 BCE); Pindar, Pythian 4.88 (c. 462 BCE).
b_naxos.eponym_details: Mythologically named after Naxos, leader of the Carians who settled the island.
b_naxos.etymology_analysis: Pre-Greek island name Naxos (Νάξος), naming the largest Cycladic island and its main town, attested from Archaic/Classical Greek sources onward.

b_thera.first_mention_attestation: Pindar, Pythian Ode 4.10–20 (462 BCE) and Herodotus, Histories 4.147–150 (c. 440 BCE).
b_thera.eponym_details: Named after the legendary Dorian leader Theras, son of Autesion (Herodotus 4.147).
b_thera.etymology_analysis: Ancient Greek Thera (Θήρα), naming the southern Cycladic island (modern Santorini) and its ancient city, attested from Pindar and Herodotus onward.

b_andros.eponym_details: Mythologically named after Andreus, a Cretan general of Rhadamanthus (Diodorus Siculus 5.79).
b_andros.etymology_analysis: Ancient Greek Andros (Ἄνδρος), naming the northernmost Cycladic island and its ancient polis, attested from Herodotus and Classical inscriptions onward.

b_tinos.first_mention_attestation: Herodotus, Histories 4.33, 6.97, and 8.66 (c. 440 BCE) as Tenos.
b_tinos.eponym_details: Mythologically named after Tenos, leader of Ionian colonists.
b_tinos.etymology_analysis: Ancient Greek Tenos (Τῆνος, Modern/Byzantine Tinos), naming the Cycladic island and its chief town, continuously attested since Herodotus.

b_rhodos.first_mention_attestation: Synoecized city of Rhodos founded in 408 BCE (Diodorus Siculus 13.75); the island name Rhodos is earlier attested in Homer, Iliad 2.654 (c. 8th century BCE).
b_rhodos.eponym_details: Mythologically linked to the nymph Rhode, daughter of Poseidon.
b_rhodos.etymology_analysis: Ancient Greek Rhodos (Ῥόδος), naming the largest Dodecanese island and its synoecized capital (founded 408 BCE), attested in Homer and Mycenaean sources.

b_kos.eponym_details: Mythologically linked to Kos, daughter of Merops.
b_kos.etymology_analysis: Pre-Greek island name Kos (Κῶς), naming the Dodecanese island and its chief polis, attested since the Iliad.

b_lindos.eponym_details: Mythologically named after Lindus, grandson of Helios.
b_lindos.etymology_analysis: Pre-Greek toponym Lindos (Λίνδος), one of the three ancient Dorian cities of Rhodes, attested in Homer's Catalogue of Ships and continuously inhabited through the Byzantine era.

b_karpathos.first_mention_attestation: Homer, Iliad 2.676 (as Krapathos, c. 8th century BCE)

morphemes.translation: Karpathos (etymology uncertain; pre-Greek Aegean island name)

b_karpathos.etymology_analysis: Pre-Greek Aegean island toponym attested in Homer (Iliad 2.676) with metathesis as Krapathos and later standardly as Karpathos.

b_athens.first_mention_attestation: Mycenaean Linear B tablet KN V 52 (a-ta-na-po-ti-ni-ja, c. 1400 BCE) and Homer, Iliad 2.546 / Odyssey 7.80 (c. 8th century BCE)

morphemes.translation: Athens (plural toponym; pre-Greek root shared with goddess Athena)

b_athens.etymology_analysis: Pre-Greek toponym attested in Mycenaean Linear B (a-ta-na) and Homeric Greek as plural Athenai; modern scholarship generally holds that the goddess Athena was named after the city.

b_thebeshellas.first_mention_attestation: Mycenaean Linear B tablets from Thebes and Pylos (te-qa-i, c. 1300 BCE) and Homer, Iliad 4.378 (c. 8th century BCE)
b_thebeshellas.etymology_analysis: Bronze Age Mycenaean toponym attested in Linear B as te-qa-i (*Thegwai), evolving into Classical Greek Thebai.

b_megara.first_mention_attestation: Theognis of Megara (6th century BCE) and Herodotus, Histories (5th century BCE)

morphemes.translation: great halls / sanctuaries / underground chambers (plural of megaron)

b_megara.etymology_analysis: Ancient Greek plural of megaron ('great hall' or 'sacred chamber/sanctuary', traditionally linked to sanctuaries of Demeter).

morphemes.translation: Lebadeia (traditionally from mythical founder Lebados; modern Greek Livadeia/Levadia)

b_levadia.etymology_analysis: Ancient Boeotian city name Lebadeia (attested in Herodotus 8.134), whose Modern Greek pronunciation yields Livadeia / Levadia.

older_name_by_867.notes: Pausanias (9.39.1) states that the city originally stood on high ground under the name Mideia (attested in Homer's Catalogue of Ships) before moving to the plain as Lebadeia.

b_boudounitsa.first_mention_attestation: Chronicle of the Morea and Frankish feudal grants establishing the Marquisate of Bodonitsa in 1204 CE
b_boudounitsa.etymology_analysis: Medieval toponym (also Bodonitsa, Vodonitsa, later Mendenitsa) of likely Slavic origin from the Middle Byzantine period, first documented in 1204 when Boniface of Montferrat granted it to Guido Pallavicini.

older_name_by_867.notes: The Frankish castle of Bodonitsa incorporates ancient ashlar blocks on an acropolis often identified with ancient Pharygai in Epicnemidian Locris.

b_amfissa.eponym_details: Mythologically linked to Amphissa, daughter of Macar and beloved of Apollo.

morphemes.translation: toponymic suffix (traditionally linked to amphiennymi 'to surround', as it is surrounded by mountains)

b_amfissa.etymology_analysis: Ancient Locrian polis name Amphissa, classically explained from amphiennymi ('to surround', referencing Mt. Giona and Mt. Parnassus) or mythical eponym Amphissa.

b_chalkis.etymology_analysis: Ancient Greek Chalkis, derived from chalkos ('copper/bronze'), attested from Homer's Catalogue of Ships (Iliad 2.537).

b_skopelos.first_mention_attestation: Claudius Ptolemy, Geography 3.13 (c. 150 CE, as Skopelos)
b_skopelos.etymology_analysis: From Ancient Greek skopelos ('lookout rock, crag, reef'), referring to the reefs around the island; first attested in Ptolemy (2nd century CE), replacing earlier Peparethos.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Homeric Hymn to Apollo 32 (c. 6th century BCE); Thucydides 3.89
older_name_by_867.notes: Throughout the Archaic, Classical, and Hellenistic periods the island and its main settlement were known as Peparethos.

b_oreoi.first_mention_attestation: Attic inscriptions / Thucydides 8.95 following the Athenian synoecism of 445 BCE (as Oreos)

morphemes.translation: Oreus (traditionally linked to the hunter Orion or mountain/border watch)

b_oreoi.etymology_analysis: Ancient Euboean town Oreos (pluralized in Modern Greek as Oreoi), which became the main city name after Pericles settled Athenian cleruchs there in 445 BCE.

older_name_by_867.notes: Prior to the 5th-century BCE synoecism (445 BCE), the city was known as Histiaia (Hestiaia), attested in the Iliad.

b_phocaea.first_mention_attestation: Herodotus, Histories 1.163 (c. 440 BCE; city founded c. 8th–7th century BCE)
b_phocaea.etymology_analysis: From Ancient Greek phoke ('seal'), reflected on Phocaean coinage depicting seals; an ancient Ionian polis founded by Phocian/Athenian colonists.

b_pergamon.etymology_analysis: Pre-Greek / Anatolian toponym cognate with Greek pergamos ('citadel'), attested historically from Xenophon's Anabasis (399 BCE) and later capital of the Attalid kingdom.

b_adramyttium.first_mention_attestation: Herodotus, Histories 7.42 (c. 440 BCE; city founded 6th century BCE)
b_adramyttium.eponym_details: Named after Adramytos, brother of Croesus and son of Lydian King Alyattes (6th century BCE), according to Aristotle.

morphemes.translation: city of Adramytos (son of Lydian king Alyattes)

b_adramyttium.etymology_analysis: Greek adaptation (Adramyttion / Latin Adramyttium) of a Lydian foundation attributed by Aristotle to Adramytos, son of King Alyattes (6th century BCE).

b_smyrna.first_mention_attestation: Mimnermus fr. 9 (7th century BCE) and Herodotus, Histories 1.149 (c. 440 BCE)

morphemes.translation: Smyrna (traditionally associated with myrrh / Amazon Smyrna; cf. Old Assyrian Ti-smurna)

b_smyrna.etymology_analysis: Ancient Anatolian/Aeolic toponym (Ionic Smyrne, Aeolic/Attic Smyrna), attested in Archaic Greek poetry (Mimnermus, 7th century BCE) and Herodotus.

b_halikarnassos.etymology_analysis: Carian-Greek toponym featuring the Anatolian/Pre-Greek -ssos suffix; famous as the birthplace of Herodotus and capital of Caria under Mausolus.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Strabo, Geography 14.2.16; Pliny the Elder, Naturalis Historia 5.29
older_name_by_867.notes: Classical geographers (Strabo, Pliny) record Zephyria as the original name of the settlement on the former island/peninsula.

b_iassus.first_mention_attestation: Thucydides, History of the Peloponnesian War 8.28 (events of 412 BCE) and Athenian Tribute Lists (5th century BCE)
b_iassus.etymology_analysis: Ancient Carian-Greek coastal city name (Iasos/Iassos, Latinized Iassus), attested in 5th-century BCE Athenian Tribute Lists and Thucydides.

b_miletus.first_mention_attestation: Hittite Annals of Mursili II (as Millawanda, c. 1320 BCE), Mycenaean Linear B (mi-ra-ti-ja, c. 1200 BCE), and Homer, Iliad 2.868 (c. 8th century BCE)
b_miletus.etymology_analysis: Bronze Age Anatolian toponym (Hittite Millawanda/Milawata), adapted into Mycenaean/Ionic Greek as Miletos (Doric/Aeolic Milatos).

b_ephesos.first_mention_attestation: Callinus of Ephesus (7th century BCE) and Herodotus, Histories 1.26 (c. 440 BCE)

morphemes.translation: Ephesus (Greek adaptation of Bronze Age Luwian/Hittite Apasa)

b_ephesos.etymology_analysis: Greek adaptation (Ephesos) of the Bronze Age Arzawan city name Apasa; attested in Greek from the 7th century BCE.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Hittite Annals of Mursili II (c. 1320 BCE)
older_name_by_867.notes: Ephesus was built on the site of Apasa, the Bronze Age capital of the kingdom of Arzawa attested in 14th–13th century BCE Hittite records.

morphemes.translation: Lebedus (one of the twelve cities of the Ionian League)

b_lebedos.etymology_analysis: Pre-Greek / Anatolian coastal toponym attested as an Ionian League polis in Herodotus 1.142.

older_name_by_867.notes: Strabo (14.1.29) records that the site previously bore the Lydian/pre-Greek name Artis.

b_brysis.first_mention_attestation: Acts of the Second Council of Nicaea (787 CE, Bishop John of Brysis; also traditionally dated to c. 425 CE under Theodosius II)
b_brysis.etymology_analysis: From Greek brysis ('spring, source of water'), later translated into Turkish as Pınarhisar ('spring-fortress'); attested as a Byzantine bishopric by 787 CE.

b_arkadiopolis.first_mention_attestation: Renamed under Eastern Roman Emperor Arcadius (r. 395–408 CE); attested in 5th–6th century Byzantine sources (e.g., Hierocles, Synecdemus)
b_arkadiopolis.eponym_details: Named after Eastern Roman Emperor Arcadius (r. 395–408 CE), who refounded the city c. 400 CE.
b_arkadiopolis.etymology_analysis: Compound of Emperor Arcadius's name and Greek polis ('City of Arcadius'), refounded c. 400 CE on the site of ancient Bergoule.

older_name_by_867.notes: Earlier Thracian/Roman town of Bergoule (Bergule/Bergula), attested in Ptolemy and the Antonine/Bordeaux Itineraries before being renamed Arkadiopolis.

b_selymbria.first_mention_attestation: Herodotus, Histories 6.33 (c. 440 BCE; Megarian colony founded c. 7th century BCE)
b_selymbria.eponym_details: Named after its legendary Thracian founder Selys (Thracian 'Selys-bria', town of Selys).
b_selymbria.etymology_analysis: Thracian compound meaning 'town of Selys' (-bria = 'town'), Hellenized as Selymbria when colonized by Megarians.

b_herakleiaperinthos.first_mention_attestation: Renamed Heraclea c. 300 CE under Diocletian (attested in Ammianus Marcellinus 27.4 and Notitia Dignitatum); combined with classical Perinthos (Herodotus 4.90)
b_herakleiaperinthos.eponym_details: Renamed Herakleia c. 300 CE in honor of Heracles (patron deity of the Herculian Tetrarchy under Diocletian and Maximian).
b_herakleiaperinthos.etymology_analysis: Late Roman name Herakleia (adopted c. 300 CE in honor of Heracles/Herculian tetrarchy) paired with the older pre-Greek/Thracian name Perinthos.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Herodotus, Histories 4.90 (c. 440 BCE; founded c. 600 BCE by Samians)
older_name_by_867.notes: Originally founded as Perinthos (Perinthus) c. 600 BCE; renamed Heraclea c. 300 CE.

b_bizye.first_mention_attestation: Strabo, Geography 7 fr. 47 (1st century BCE/CE) and late 1st-century BCE Thracian inscriptions

morphemes.translation: Bizye (royal residence of the Thracian Asti)

b_bizye.etymology_analysis: Thracian toponym (Greek Bizye, modern Turkish Vize), attested from the 1st century BCE/CE as the royal capital of the Thracian Asti tribe.

b_salmydessus.first_mention_attestation: Aeschylus, Prometheus Bound 726 (c. 460 BCE) and Herodotus, Histories 4.93 (c. 440 BCE)

morphemes.translation: Salmydessus (coastal district and town on the Black Sea)

b_salmydessus.etymology_analysis: Pre-Greek / Thracian toponym with -ssos suffix, attested in 5th-century BCE Greek sources (Aeschylus, Herodotus, Xenophon) for the dangerous Black Sea coast and town.

b_constantinople.first_mention_attestation: Dedicated as Constantinopolis by Emperor Constantine I on 11 May 330 CE
b_constantinople.eponym_details: Named after Roman Emperor Constantine I (Constantine the Great), who dedicated Constantinopolis as the new imperial capital on 11 May 330 CE.
b_constantinople.etymology_analysis: Greek Konstantinoupolis / Latin Constantinopolis ('City of Constantine'), dedicated in 330 CE as the new imperial capital on the site of Byzantion.

older_name_by_867.first_mention_source: Herodotus, Histories 4.144 (c. 440 BCE; Megarian colony founded c. 657 BCE)
older_name_by_867.notes: Founded as a Megarian colony under the name Byzantion (Latin Byzantium) in the 7th century BCE before Constantine I refounded it as Constantinople in 324–330 CE.

b_kalliopolis.first_mention_attestation: Athenian Tribute Lists (434 BCE, as Kallipolitai) and Livy, History of Rome 31.16 (events of 200 BCE)
b_kalliopolis.etymology_analysis: Ancient Greek Kallipolis ('beautiful city'), attested from the 5th century BCE in the Athenian Tribute Lists and later Latinized as Callipolis / Italian Gallipoli / Turkish Gelibolu.

b_ainos.first_mention_attestation: Homer, Iliad 4.520 (c. 8th century BCE, as Ainos)
b_ainos.etymology_analysis: Ancient Greek city name attested in Homer (Iliad 4.520), colonized by Aeolians from Mytilene and Kyme at the mouth of the Hebrus.

older_name_by_867.notes: Classical sources (Strabo, Stephanus of Byzantium) record Poltymbria / Poltyobria ('town of Poltys') as the earlier Thracian name of the site.

b_kypsela.first_mention_attestation: Coins of Thracian ruler Adaios minted at Kypsela (c. 255–245 BCE) and Strabo, Geography 7 fr. 47

morphemes.translation: hollow vessel, beehive (or named after a Thracian/Greek Cypselus)

b_kypsela.etymology_analysis: Ancient Greek Kypsela (Latin Cypsela, modern Turkish Ipsala), attested from the 3rd century BCE as a key Thracian city and Via Egnatia station on the Hebrus.

b_raidestos.first_mention_attestation: Procopius, De Aedificiis 4.9 (c. 550 CE, as Rhaedestus / Raidestos; cf. Pliny NH 4.11 Resisto, c. 77 CE)
b_raidestos.etymology_analysis: Late Roman/Byzantine name Raidestos (Latinized Rhaedestus), attested by Procopius in the 6th century CE as the successor name to ancient Bisanthe.

older_name_by_867.notes: Founded by Samian colonists and attested as Bisanthe in Herodotus and Xenophon before being renamed Rhaedestus/Raidestos by Late Antiquity.

b_chariopolis.first_mention_attestation: Acts of the Second Council of Nicaea (787 CE, Bishop Theophylact of Chariopolis)
b_chariopolis.etymology_analysis: Byzantine Greek compound Chariopolis ('City of Grace/Joy'), first attested at the Second Council of Nicaea in 787 CE and later Ottoman Hayrabolu.
